abstract: |
  I analyse 53,907 political-violence events recorded by ACLED in Myanmar between
  1 January 2021 and 30 September 2025, counted in each of the 330 townships of the
  MIMU 9.4 boundary set, and ask three questions: where violence clusters, how its
  geography is changing, and whether it spreads from one township to the next.

  Violence is strongly clustered. Global Moran's I sits between 0.56 and 0.71 for
  every variable. Local Moran's I and Gi* agree on one dominant core, the
  central dry zone of Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay, which holds between half and nine in ten of the significant High-High
  townships depending on the event type, with a second belt
  running down the Thai border through Kayin, Mon and Tanintharyi. The cold spots
  are the Ayeyarwady delta, Yangon and the eastern Shan hills, and I argue that the
  last of these is partly an artefact of reporting rather than peace.

  Over time the picture is of a war that has stopped spreading outward from cities
  and is deepening where it already is. Yangon's townships show a significant
  downward Gi* trend almost without exception. The intensifying hot spots are in
  the dry zone (Madaya, Myingyan, Seikphyu, Yesagyo, Ngazun) and at Dawei, and the
  consecutive hot spots trace the southeastern front from Kyaukkyi to Myawaddy.
  Explosions and remote violence, increasingly air and drone strikes by the
  military, overtook battles as the most common event type in 2023.

  As a value-added analysis I fitted a spatial Markov model. A quiet township
  becomes active in the next quarter 9% of the time when no neighbour is active and
  36% of the time when most neighbours are, a gap that survives a spatial
  permutation test, state and quarter fixed effects, and three activity thresholds.
  Since Operation 1027 an isolated outbreak has become rarer (12% to 4%) while
  spread into a township surrounded by fighting has not changed, which is the
  signature of a war fought along contiguous fronts.

```{r setup}
#| include: false

  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(sf); library(ggplot2); library(glue)

})

P <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "prepared.rds"))
L <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "lmsa.rds"))
E <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "ehsa.rds"))
D <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "diffusion.rds"))
G <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "ehsa_gi.rds"))

tsp <- P$tsp
ev  <- P$ev
states <- tsp |> group_by(ST) |> summarise(.groups = "drop")
bb <- st_bbox(tsp)
tsp_attr <- st_drop_geometry(tsp) |> select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST, area_km2, pv)

with_geo <- function(df) tsp |> select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) |> left_join(df, by = "TS_PCODE")
var_lab <- function(v) factor(VAR_LABELS[v], levels = VAR_LABELS)
coarse <- function(x) case_when(grepl("hotspot", x) ~ "hot", grepl("coldspot", x) ~ "cold", TRUE ~ "none")

# numbers quoted in the prose
n_ev   <- nrow(ev)
qa     <- P$qa
glob   <- L$global
lisa_n <- L$lisa |> count(var, cls)
hh_pv  <- L$lisa |> filter(var == "pv", cls == "High-High") |> left_join(tsp_attr, by = "TS_PCODE")
ehsa_pv <- E$ehsa |> filter(var == "pv") |> left_join(tsp_attr, by = "TS_PCODE")
mk_pv  <- E$mk |> filter(var == "pv") |> left_join(tsp_attr, by = "TS_PCODE")
tb     <- D$tab
on_none <- tb$p_active_next[tb$from == "Quiet" & tb$ctx == D$ctx_lab[1]]
on_most <- tb$p_active_next[tb$from == "Quiet" & tb$ctx == D$ctx_lab[3]]
or_most <- D$or_tab |> filter(term == "ctxMost neighbours active")
```

# Introduction and study context

Myanmar has been at war with parts of itself since independence in 1948, mostly as a
contest between the national army, the Tatmadaw, and ethnic armed organisations in
the hills that ring the central plain. The coup of 1 February 2021 changed the shape
of that war. When peaceful protest was met with live fire, a generation of young
people in the Bamar heartland, which had been largely spared the ethnic conflicts,
took up arms as local People's Defence Forces. The war came to the plains.

That shift is what makes this exercise a geographical question rather than only a
humanitarian one. Before 2021 the map of violence was largely the map of the
borderlands. Since 2021 it has had to be redrawn, and it has kept moving: urban
resistance in Yangon in 2021, the rise of the dry-zone insurgency in Sagaing and
Magway, the Arakan Army's offensive in Rakhine, and Operation 1027, the Three
Brotherhood Alliance offensive that began in northern Shan on 27 October 2023 and
cost the military more territory in months than it had lost in decades.

Peace-building organisations work at township level. Township is the unit at which
humanitarian access is negotiated, aid is planned and local ceasefires are
brokered, and it is the finest administrative unit for which boundaries are
maintained consistently, by the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU). So I
analyse the conflict at that scale, and I ask what a peace-building organisation
could defensibly do with the result.

# Research question and objectives

**Where does armed conflict in Myanmar cluster, how is that geography changing, and
does it spread from township to township?**

1. Locate statistically significant hot spots, cold spots and spatial outliers of
   political violence at township level, separately for battles, explosions and
   remote violence, violence against civilians, and reported fatalities
   (Local Moran's I and Getis-Ord Gi*).
2. Describe where, how fast and in what pattern the geography is evolving, using a
   quarterly space-time cube, the Mann-Kendall trend test on each township's Gi*
   series, and emerging hot spot analysis (EHSA).
3. *Value-added.* Test whether violence diffuses by contagion: whether a quiet
   township is more likely to become violent when its neighbours already are, after
   allowing for regional and national conditions (a spatial Markov chain).

# Data and study design

```{r tbl-data}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Inputs. Neither is committed to the repository: ACLED's terms do not allow redistribution, and the README records how to obtain both."
tribble(
  ~Dataset, ~Source, ~Content, ~Used.as,
  "ACLED Myanmar extract", "Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, via eLearn",
  glue("{fmt_n(qa$n_raw)} events, 1 Jan 2021 to 30 Sep 2025, 31 fields"), "Point events, aggregated to counts",
  "Township boundaries", "MIMU GeoNode, PCode release 9.4",
  glue("{nrow(tsp)} townships, 1:250,000, WGS 84"), "Areal unit and spatial weights"
) |> kable(col.names = c("Dataset", "Source", "Content", "Used as"))
```

**Unit of analysis.** The township. Its boundaries come from MIMU release 9.4,
verified from the `PCode_V` field on every polygon. I fetch them directly from
MIMU's WFS endpoint inside the pipeline, so the version is not in doubt.

**What counts as armed conflict.** ACLED codes six event types. I keep the three it
groups as political violence: *battles*, *explosions/remote violence* and
*violence against civilians*. *Protests* and *riots* are not armed conflict, and
*strategic developments* (arrests, base movements, territory changing hands without
fighting) are not violent events. Mixing them in would let the 2021 protest wave
dominate the early quarters for reasons unrelated to the war.

**Variables.** Five counts per township: all political violence, each of the three
types, and the sum of reported fatalities.

**Space-time cube.** Township by calendar quarter: `r nrow(tsp)` townships by
`r length(P$quarters)` quarters, `r fmt_n(nrow(P$cube))` cells, with an explicit
zero wherever nothing was recorded. The study window ends on 30 September 2025,
the last day of a quarter, so there is no partial final period. I chose quarters
over months for three reasons. About `r fmt_pct((qa$time_prec$n[2] + qa$time_prec$n[3]) / sum(qa$time_prec$n), 1)`
of events are dated only to the week or month, which a month boundary would split
arbitrarily. A monthly cube is mostly zeros in quiet townships, which gives the
Mann-Kendall test little to work with. And a quarter matches the planning cycle of
the organisations this is meant for. I rebuild the analysis on a monthly cube as a
check (@sec-ehsa-sens).

**Projection.** WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647). Myanmar's centroid, about
96.5°E, lies in zone 47. Contiguity does not need a projection, but the snapping
distance, the nearest-neighbour weights and township areas do.

# Data preparation and quality assessment

The brief warns that the data are full of land mines. These are the ones I found,
in the order the pipeline meets them.

```{r tbl-audit}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Audit trail from R/01_prepare.R. Every row removed is accounted for. The large drop at step three is the deliberate exclusion of protests, riots and strategic developments, not a quality loss."
P$audit |> mutate(removed = if_else(is.na(removed), "", fmt_n(removed)), rows = fmt_n(rows)) |>
  select(Step = step, `Rows remaining` = rows, Removed = removed, Reason = why) |> kable()
```

**Events in the sea.** `r qa$indian_ocean` rows have `country = "Indian Ocean"`.
They are maritime incidents ACLED attaches to the Myanmar file. I removed them
by the country field rather than letting the spatial join decide, so the reason
is on record.

**Events placed on a regional centroid.** ACLED's `geo_precision` is 1 when the
event is located to a named town or village, 2 when it is near one, and 3 when
only the larger region is known and the event is placed at that region's
centroid. Political violence has `r qa$geo3_pv` events at precision 3. Counting
them would pile false violence onto whichever township contains a district's
centroid, so I drop them. At 0.2% of events, the loss is small; the distortion
from keeping them would not be.

**Join by location, not by name.** ACLED records its own `admin3` name for each
event, and it is tempting to join on it. `r fmt_n(qa$admin3_na_pv)` political-violence
rows have no `admin3` at all, and names are romanised inconsistently across
sources. So I join every event to the township polygon that contains its
coordinates, and use the names only to audit the join afterwards
(@tbl-names). The agreement is reassuring: ACLED evidently codes against MIMU's own
gazetteer, and only `r qa$name_mismatch_events` events carry a name that differs
from the township they fall in, each a point that lies a few hundred metres across
a boundary. The `r qa$name_na_events` events with no name all fall in the city
townships of Mandalay, Yangon and Nay Pyi Taw, and the spatial join recovers them.
A name join would have lost every one.

```{r tbl-names}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Every case where ACLED's township name disagrees with the township its coordinates fall in, or is missing. All other events agree."
P$names_chk |> filter(!match | is.na(match)) |>
  mutate(admin3 = coalesce(admin3, "(missing)")) |>
  select(`ACLED admin3` = admin3, `Spatial join` = TS, Events = events) |> kable()
```

**Points just off the coast.** `r nrow(qa$snapped)` events fall outside every
polygon. All are on islands or river mouths that the 1:250,000 coastline
generalises away, the furthest `r round(max(qa$snapped$dist_km), 2)` km from land.
I snap events to the nearest township within `r SNAP_TOLERANCE_M / 1000` km, which
recovers all eight without risking real offshore incidents.

**Fatalities are not like the counts.** ACLED codes fatalities conservatively and
from reports, and Myanmar's reporting environment is hostile. The distribution is
extreme: the top 1% of events account for
`r fmt_pct(qa$fat_share_top1pct)` of all reported deaths, and the largest single
values (400, 350, 201) are territorial takeovers in Rakhine and Shan where the
death toll covers weeks of fighting. I keep fatalities as a variable because
lethality matters for protection work, but I treat its local statistics as less
reliable than the event counts, and I never use it to build the space-time cube.

**Zeros that may not be zeros.** `r qa$zero_tsp` townships record no political
violence at all in nearly five years. Seven of them are in the Wa and Mongla
self-administered areas of eastern and northern Shan, held by the United Wa State
Army and the National Democratic Alliance Army, ceasefire groups that tightly
control information. The eighth is Cocokyun, a small island. A zero in Wa territory
partly reflects calm under ceasefire, but it also reflects that almost nothing is
reported from there. This matters later, because those townships anchor a cold
spot.

```{r fig-coverage}
#| fig-cap: "Political-violence events per township, January 2021 to September 2025, on a square-root scale so that the many moderate townships are not washed out by the few extreme ones. State and region boundaries in black."
#| fig-height: 7.6
#| fig-width: 7.2
lab <- states |> st_point_on_surface() |>
  mutate(ST = sub(" \\(", "\n(", ST))
ggplot(tsp) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pv), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf_label(data = lab, aes(label = ST), size = 2.3, colour = PAL$ink,
                family = "Helvetica", lineheight = 0.9, fill = alpha("#FFFFFF", 0.75),
                label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(1.2, "pt")) +
  scale_fill_count(name = "Political-violence events", v = tsp$pv) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map() +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(40, "pt"))
```

The map has a clear centre of gravity. The densest band of townships runs through
the central dry zone, the lowland Bamar heartland of southern Sagaing, Magway and
Mandalay, which until 2021 had seen little armed conflict. Monywa and Kale in Sagaing and Myaing in Magway are three of the five busiest
townships in the country, each with more than 850 events; the other two are
Kawkareik on the Thai border and Hpakant in Kachin's jade-mining district. A second band follows the Thai border south through
Kayin, Mon and Tanintharyi. The quietest areas are the Ayeyarwady delta, the
Yangon hinterland and eastern Shan. Kachin and northern Shan are active, but the
activity concentrates in fewer townships.

Raw counts reward size. Large townships have more room for events, and the
choropleth's eye is drawn to them. That is acceptable for this purpose, because
the township is the unit at which programmes operate, but it is the reason I rely
on the local statistics below rather than on this map to say where violence is
unusual.

# Analytical assumptions and methodological decisions

```{r tbl-decisions}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Decisions that shape every result after this point, with the alternative I tested where one exists."
tribble(
  ~Decision, ~Choice, ~Why, ~Checked.against,
  "Neighbours", "Queen contiguity, row-standardised", "Townships interact across shared borders; a fighting front crosses them", glue("{K_SENS}-nearest neighbours"),
  "Islands", "Linked to nearest township", glue("{nrow(L$w_info$islands)} townships share no boundary; dropping them removes real places"), "-",
  "Transformation", "log(1 + count)", "Counts are heavily skewed; extremes would decide whole neighbourhoods", "Raw counts",
  "Inference", glue("{NSIM_LMSA} conditional permutations"), "No normality assumption for skewed counts", "-",
  "Significance", "p < 0.05, as the brief requires", "Reported alongside the false discovery rate", "FDR-adjusted p",
  "Time step", "Calendar quarter", "Week- and month-dated events; sparse monthly series", "Monthly cube",
  "EHSA rule threshold", "0.05", "sfdep defaults to 0.01; the brief sets 0.05", "-"
) |> kable(col.names = c("Decision", "Choice", "Why", "Checked against"))
```

**Spatial weights.** Queen contiguity treats two townships as neighbours if they
share any boundary point. That is the natural definition for conflict, which moves
across land borders along roads and rivers. `r nrow(L$w_info$islands)` townships
have no contiguous neighbour: `r paste(L$w_info$islands$TS, collapse = ", ")`. Left
alone, they would split the network into four disconnected pieces and give the
permutation tests empty rows. I link each to its nearest township by centroid
(`r paste(glue("{L$w_info$islands$TS} to {L$w_info$islands$linked_to}"), collapse = "; ")`)
and make the links symmetric, which leaves one connected network with a median of
`r median(L$w_info$card)` neighbours. For Gi* each township is also included in its
own neighbourhood, which is what distinguishes Gi* from Gi.

**Transformation.** Political-violence counts run from 0 to
`r fmt_n(max(tsp$pv))` with a median of `r fmt_n(median(tsp$pv))`. Local Moran's I
is a product of a township's deviation from the mean and its neighbours'. On raw
counts, Monywa's 1,039 events would make every neighbour of Monywa look like part
of a cluster whatever its own level. Taking log(1 + count) keeps the ordering and
the zeros, and lets the statistic describe the bulk of townships rather than the
five largest. I re-ran everything on raw counts to see what changes
(@tbl-sens).

**Permutation inference.** Analytical p-values for Local Moran's I assume
normality, which skewed counts violate. I use conditional permutation instead:
each township's value is held fixed while its neighbours' values are drawn at
random from the rest of the map `r NSIM_LMSA` times, so the smallest attainable
p-value is 0.001.

**Many tests at once.** Testing 330 townships at 5% will produce about 16 false
positives by chance alone. The brief asks for the p < 0.05 maps and I give them, but
I also report how many townships survive a false discovery rate correction, so the
reader can see which clusters are robust and which are at the margin.

# Geographical distribution over time

```{r fig-series}
#| fig-cap: "Political-violence events per month by type, with the coup and the start of Operation 1027 marked. The second panel isolates the military's air and drone strikes, which are counted inside explosions and remote violence."
#| fig-height: 5.6
mon <- qa$monthly |> mutate(type = var_lab(var))
air <- st_drop_geometry(ev) |> filter(sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike") |> count(month)
type_cols <- c(PAL$accent, "#D0543F", PAL$cool) |> setNames(VAR_LABELS[c("battles", "erv", "vac")])
marks <- list(
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(COUP_DATE, OP1027_DATE), colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "22"),
  annotate("text", x = c(COUP_DATE, OP1027_DATE) + 20, y = Inf, vjust = 1.4, hjust = 0,
           label = c("Coup", "Operation 1027"), size = 2.9, colour = PAL$muted, family = "Helvetica"))
p1 <- ggplot(mon, aes(month, n, colour = type)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.55) + marks +
  scale_colour_manual(values = type_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Events per month") + theme_ex02()
p2 <- ggplot(air, aes(month, n)) + geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_dk, width = 25) + marks[1] +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Air and drone\nstrikes") + theme_ex02()
p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(2.2, 1))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
yr <- st_drop_geometry(ev) |> mutate(y = format(event_date, "%Y")) |>
  group_by(y) |> summarise(air = sum(sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike"),
                           mil_erv = mean(grepl("Military Forces", actor1)[var == "erv"]),
                           n_b = sum(var == "battles"), n_e = sum(var == "erv"))
```

Violence climbed steeply through 2021 as the armed resistance formed, then held at
around 1,000 events a month (between 824 and 1,126) from 2022 until the autumn of 2023. Operation 1027 produced the
largest spike in the record, in November 2023, and the level has eased since,
though in 2025 it is still above anything in 2021.

The composition changed more than the level. Explosions and remote violence
overtook battles as the most common event type during 2023 and stayed ahead. Behind
that crossing is the military's turn to the air. ACLED records
`r yr$air[yr$y == "2021"]` air or drone strikes in 2021 and
`r fmt_n(yr$air[yr$y == "2024"])` in 2024. The share of explosions and remote
violence initiated by the military rose from
`r fmt_pct(yr$mil_erv[yr$y == "2021"])` to `r fmt_pct(yr$mil_erv[yr$y == "2025"])`
in 2025. Violence against civilians, by contrast, fell as a share of the total.
The war became one fought from a distance, which matters for the maps that follow,
because an air strike lands where the military chooses to strike, not where the
fighting is.

```{r fig-states}
#| fig-cap: "Quarterly political-violence events by state and region. Each row is scaled to its own maximum so the timing of each region's surge is visible regardless of its size; the number at right is the region's total."
#| fig-height: 5.8
sq <- P$cube |> left_join(tsp_attr |> select(TS_PCODE, ST), by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  group_by(ST, period) |> summarise(pv = sum(pv), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(ST) |> mutate(rel = pv / max(pv), tot = sum(pv)) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(ST = reorder(ST, tot))
tots <- sq |> distinct(ST, tot)
ggplot(sq, aes(period, ST, fill = rel)) +
  geom_tile(colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.4, height = 0.92) +
  geom_text(data = tots, aes(x = max(sq$period) + 75, y = ST, label = fmt_n(tot)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, size = 2.7, colour = PAL$muted, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Share of the region's busiest quarter",
                       labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y", expand = expansion(add = c(0, 260))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_ex02(grid = "none") +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(40, "pt"))
```

Each region has its own clock. Yangon peaked in the first year, when the
resistance was an urban one of bombings and targeted killings, and has faded ever
since. Sagaing, the single largest theatre, ramped up through 2021 and peaked in
2022. Rakhine was nearly silent until a brief round of fighting in late 2022, then
the Arakan Army's offensive from November 2023 turned it into one of the most
violent regions in the country. Northern Shan peaks sharply in the Operation 1027
quarter and settles after the ceasefire brokered by China in January 2024. Kachin is
the opposite case, busiest in 2021 Q2. Mandalay, Magway, Bago West and Kayin reach
their busiest quarters only in 2024 or 2025.

These different clocks are the reason a single map of five-year totals is not
enough, and the reason the space-time analysis in @sec-ehsa is needed.

# Local measures of spatial association

## Global autocorrelation first

```{r tbl-global}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Global Moran's I on log(1 + count), queen contiguity, 999 permutations. Every variable is strongly and significantly clustered."
glob |> mutate(Variable = VAR_LABELS[var], I = round(I, 3),
               p = map_chr(p_sim, fmt_p, nperm = NSIM_LMSA)) |>
  select(Variable, `Moran's I` = I, `Permutation p` = p) |> kable()
```

Global Moran's I between `r round(min(glob$I), 2)` and `r round(max(glob$I), 2)`
says that a township's violence is very well predicted by its neighbours'. That
justifies looking for local clusters, but on its own says nothing about where they
are.

## Local Moran's I

```{r fig-lisa}
#| fig-cap: "Local Moran's I cluster maps, p < 0.05 by conditional permutation (999). Only significant townships are coloured. High-High: a violent township among violent neighbours. Low-Low: a quiet township among quiet neighbours. Low-High: a quiet township surrounded by violence. No High-Low outlier reaches significance for any variable."
#| fig-height: 6.2
lm <- with_geo(L$lisa) |> mutate(var = var_lab(var), cls = factor(cls, names(LISA_COLS())))
ggplot(lm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cls), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.18) +
  facet_wrap(~var, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = LISA_COLS(), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
lisa_tab <- L$lisa |> group_by(var) |>
  summarise(HH = sum(cls == "High-High"), LL = sum(cls == "Low-Low"),
            LH = sum(cls == "Low-High"), HL = sum(cls == "High-Low"),
            sig = sum(sig), fdr = sum(p_fdr < ALPHA))
hh_dz <- L$lisa |> filter(cls == "High-High") |> left_join(tsp_attr, by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  group_by(var) |> summarise(share = mean(ST %in% c("Sagaing", "Magway", "Mandalay")))
```

**What the maps say.** For every variable the largest High-High cluster is the
same block of the dry zone: southern Sagaing, northern Magway and western
Mandalay. Between `r fmt_pct(min(hh_dz$share))` and `r fmt_pct(max(hh_dz$share))`
of each variable's High-High townships lie in those three regions. A second
High-High belt runs down the eastern border from Kayin through Mon to Tanintharyi.
Battles add a western belt in Chin and a northern patch in Kachin, matching the
ethnic armed organisations there; violence against civilians is the most
concentrated, almost entirely in the dry zone and Tanintharyi.

Low-Low clusters fall in eastern Shan (including the Wa and Mongla areas
discussed above), the Ayeyarwady delta and around Yangon, and in the far north of
Kachin for explosions and civilian targeting. The few Low-High townships, such as
Hlaingbwe in Kayin and Mabein in Shan, are quieter places beside intense fighting:
candidates for watching rather than for reassurance.

There are no significant High-Low outliers at all. Violence in Myanmar does not
form isolated islands. Wherever a township is unusually violent, its neighbours are
too.

## Getis-Ord Gi*

```{r fig-gi}
#| fig-cap: "Gi* hot and cold spots on log(1 + count), each township included in its own neighbourhood, p < 0.05 by conditional permutation (999)."
#| fig-height: 6.2
gm <- with_geo(L$gi) |> mutate(var = var_lab(var), cls = factor(cls, names(GI_COLS())))
ggplot(gm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cls), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.18) +
  facet_wrap(~var, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GI_COLS(), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10)
```

Gi* asks a narrower question than Local Moran's I: is the neighbourhood total
unusually high or low? Because it does not separate a township from its
surroundings it cannot detect outliers, and here that costs little, because there
are almost none. It agrees with the Local Moran maps township for township in most
places: the dry zone and the southeastern border are hot, eastern Shan, the delta
and Yangon are cold. Its value is as a check that the clusters do not depend on
the choice of statistic, and as the quantity EHSA tracks through time.

## How robust are the clusters?

```{r tbl-sens}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Share of townships keeping the same class when one decision changes, and the count of townships significant at p < 0.05 and after a false discovery rate correction. Agreement includes townships that stay not significant."
L$sens |> left_join(lisa_tab |> select(var, sig, fdr), by = "var") |>
  transmute(Variable = VAR_LABELS[var],
            `LISA, raw counts` = fmt_pct(lisa_raw), `LISA, 6-NN` = fmt_pct(lisa_knn),
            `Gi*, raw counts` = fmt_pct(gi_raw), `Gi*, 6-NN` = fmt_pct(gi_knn),
            `High-High (log / raw / 6-NN)` = glue("{hh_base} / {hh_raw} / {hh_knn}"),
            `Significant (p<0.05 / FDR)` = glue("{sig} / {fdr}")) |> kable()
```

Between `r fmt_pct(min(unlist(L$sens[, 2:5])))` and
`r fmt_pct(max(unlist(L$sens[, 2:5])))` of townships keep their class when the
weights or the transformation change. The two changes move results in opposite
directions. Raw counts shrink the High-High set, as expected, because only the
most extreme townships and their immediate neighbours stand out. Nearest-neighbour
weights enlarge it slightly, because a fixed six neighbours reach further in the
dense centre than queen contiguity does. The core of the dry-zone cluster survives
all three versions. What changes is its fringe.

The false discovery rate correction is the sterner test. Roughly half the
townships significant at p < 0.05 survive it. Those that do are the cores of the
clusters, not their margins, which is the honest way to read the maps above: the
location of the clusters is not in doubt; the exact boundary of each is.

# Emerging hot spot analysis {#sec-ehsa}

## From a five-year snapshot to a time series

The local statistics above collapse nearly five years into one number per township.
To see change, I compute Gi* for every township in every one of the 19 quarters,
and then test each township's 19-value series for a monotonic trend with the
Mann-Kendall test. A positive and significant tau means the township's
neighbourhood has been getting hotter relative to the rest of the country; a
negative one means it has been cooling.

```{r fig-mk}
#| fig-cap: "Mann-Kendall trend in each township's quarterly Gi* series for all political violence, 2021 Q1 to 2025 Q3. Townships with p ≥ 0.05 are shown in grey. The trend is relative: a falling Gi* means the neighbourhood is becoming less violent compared with the rest of Myanmar."
#| fig-height: 7.4
#| fig-width: 7
mkm <- with_geo(E$mk |> filter(var == "pv")) |>
  mutate(fill = if_else(sl < ALPHA, tau, NA_real_))
ggplot(mkm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fill), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL$cool, mid = PAL$ground, high = PAL$accent_dk, midpoint = 0,
                       na.value = PAL$null, limits = c(-1, 1),
                       name = "Kendall's tau (p < 0.05)") +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map() +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(40, "pt"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
mk_n <- mk_pv |> count(trend)
ygn <- mk_pv |> filter(ST == "Yangon") |> count(trend)
```

`r mk_n$n[mk_n$trend == "Rising"]` townships have a significantly rising Gi* and
`r mk_n$n[mk_n$trend == "Falling"]` a falling one. The falling trend is
overwhelmingly one city: `r ygn$n[ygn$trend == "Falling"]` of Yangon Region's
`r sum(ygn$n)` townships are cooling, the signature of the urban resistance of
2021 being suppressed or pushed out. Smaller falling patches sit in Kachin
(Myitkyina, Hpakant and their neighbours) and in the city townships of Mandalay.

The rising townships form a belt across the middle of the country: Bago West, Magway,
Mandalay and Bago East, with Tanintharyi in the south and a handful in Rakhine.
These are the places where the war arrived late, either as the dry-zone
insurgency spread south and east out of Sagaing or as new fronts opened. Sagaing
itself, the largest theatre, shows almost no significant trend, because it was hot
from 2021 onward and stayed hot. A trend test cannot see a level, which is
exactly the gap EHSA fills.

## EHSA classification

EHSA combines the two pieces of information above: how often a township is a
significant Gi* hot or cold spot, and whether its Gi* is trending. I use sfdep's
implementation, which also lets each township's neighbourhood in quarter *t*
include its neighbours in quarter *t − 1*, so a hot spot must be hot in space and
persist in time. I set the significance used inside the classification rules to
0.05, as the brief does, instead of sfdep's default of 0.01.

**Checking the labels.** sfdep 0.2.5 has a defect I found in Hands-on Exercise 6:
`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` computes results in alphabetical order of location
but labels them in the geometry's order, so whenever the two differ, the
classifications land on the wrong townships with no error. I sort the townships by
PCode before building the cube, assert in the script that the orders match, and
then check the labels against the independently computed mean Gi* of each
township:

```{r tbl-check}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Mean quarterly Gi* of the townships in each EHSA group. If the labels were attached to the wrong places, hot spot classes would not have clearly positive Gi* and cold spot classes clearly negative."
E$check |> mutate(Variable = VAR_LABELS[var], kind = recode(kind, hot = "Hot spot classes",
                                                             cold = "Cold spot classes", none = "No pattern"),
                  mean_gi = round(mean_gi, 2)) |>
  select(Variable, Group = kind, Townships = n, `Mean Gi*` = mean_gi) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Group, values_from = c(Townships, `Mean Gi*`), names_glue = "{Group}: {.value}") |>
  kable()
```

```{r fig-ehsa}
#| fig-cap: "Emerging hot spot classification of all political violence, 19 quarters, Gi* with a one-quarter time lag, 199 permutations per quarter, classification rules at α = 0.05. Left: every township's class. Right: the same classes shown only where the Mann-Kendall trend is significant at p < 0.05, which is the filter the brief asks for."
#| fig-height: 7.2
em <- with_geo(E$ehsa |> filter(var == "pv")) |>
  mutate(classification = factor(classification, EHSA_LEVELS))
present <- levels(droplevels(em$classification))
em2 <- bind_rows(
  em |> mutate(panel = "All classes"),
  em |> mutate(panel = "Mann-Kendall p < 0.05 only",
               classification = if_else(p_value < ALPHA, classification, factor(NA, EHSA_LEVELS))))
ggplot(em2) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = classification), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = EHSA_COLS()[present], breaks = present, labels = ehsa_label(present),
                    name = NULL, na.value = "#FFFFFF", drop = TRUE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.width = unit(12, "pt"), legend.key.height = unit(10, "pt"))
```

```{r fig-ehsa-bar}
#| fig-cap: "Townships in each EHSA class, all political violence."
#| fig-height: 3.6
eb <- E$ehsa |> filter(var == "pv") |> count(classification) |>
  mutate(classification = factor(classification, rev(EHSA_LEVELS)))
ggplot(eb, aes(n, classification, fill = classification)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = EHSA_COLS(), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = ehsa_label) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "Townships", y = NULL) + theme_ex02(grid = "x")
```

**On the brief's filter.** The right-hand panel shows only townships whose
Mann-Kendall p is below 0.05, as the brief asks. It is worth seeing what that
removes. A *persistent* hot or cold spot is defined as one that is significant in
at least 90% of periods *without* a significant trend, so the filter deletes every
persistent class by construction: all `r sum(ehsa_pv$classification == "persistent coldspot")`
persistent cold spots vanish. The filter answers "where is the pattern changing?",
which is a good question, but it should not be read as "where is the pattern
significant". I interpret the left-hand panel and use the right-hand one to pick
out the townships whose trajectory is statistically clear.

### Interpreting the hot spot classes

```{r}
#| include: false
cls_ts <- function(c) ehsa_pv |> filter(classification == c) |> arrange(desc(pv))
osc_st <- cls_ts("oscilating hotspot") |> count(ST, sort = TRUE)
spo_st <- cls_ts("sporadic hotspot") |> count(ST, sort = TRUE)
osc_q1 <- G |> filter(t == 1, p_sim < ALPHA, gi < 0,
                      TS_PCODE %in% cls_ts("oscilating hotspot")$TS_PCODE) |> nrow()
```

**Intensifying hot spots** (`r nrow(cls_ts("intensifying hotspot"))` townships:
`r paste(cls_ts("intensifying hotspot")$TS, collapse = ", ")`). These are the
townships that have been significant hot spots in at least 90% of quarters *and*
whose Gi* is still rising. Five of the six are in the dry zone, along the
Mandalay-Magway corridor south of Sagaing, the area into which the Sagaing
insurgency has expanded; the sixth, Dawei, is the main town of northern
Tanintharyi. For a peace-building organisation this is the most urgent class:
established violence that is not plateauing. Madaya, just north of Mandalay city,
stands out with nearly 800 events and a tau of 0.71.

**Consecutive hot spots** (`r nrow(cls_ts("consecutive hotspot"))`:
`r paste(cls_ts("consecutive hotspot")$TS, collapse = ", ")`). Townships that
became hot spots and have stayed hot for an unbroken run up to the latest quarter,
after earlier periods of not being one. They trace one geographic line: the
southeastern front from Kyaukkyi and Shwegyin in Bago East, through Kyaikto and
Bilin in Mon, to Kawkareik, Myawaddy and Kyainseikgyi along the Thai border, and
on into Tanintharyi. Much of it is territory contested by the Karen National
Union, whose 2024 offensive reached Myawaddy, the main land crossing to Thailand.
Kyaukme in northern Shan, on the Operation 1027 front, is the outlier.
This is the clearest evidence in the analysis of a front that has *moved* into new
townships and stayed there.

**Oscillating hot spots** (`r nrow(cls_ts("oscilating hotspot"))`, led by
`r paste(glue("{osc_st$ST[1:3]} ({osc_st$n[1:3]})"), collapse = ", ")`). Hot in
the latest quarter but significantly cold at some earlier point. Most are in
Sagaing and Magway, which seems paradoxical for the heartland of the war. The
explanation is the start of the window. EHSA classifies on its own space-time
Gi*, and in that series `r osc_q1` of the `r nrow(cls_ts("oscilating hotspot"))`
oscillating townships were significantly cold in 2021 Q1, the quarter of the coup,
before the armed resistance existed, when the conflict was still carried by the
border regions. The first quarter is also the only one with no preceding quarter to
lag on, so its neighbourhood is purely spatial. So "oscillating" here means "transformed": quiet
farming townships that became the war's centre. That is a substantive finding, and
a warning about reading EHSA labels off a window that starts at a regime change.

**Sporadic hot spots** (`r nrow(cls_ts("sporadic hotspot"))`, led by
`r paste(glue("{spo_st$ST[1:3]} ({spo_st$n[1:3]})"), collapse = ", ")`).
On-and-off hot spots that were never cold. Northern Shan and Kachin dominate: front
lines that flare with offensives and go quiet under local ceasefires, as northern
Shan did after the China-brokered truce of January 2024.

**Diminishing hot spot.** One township, Gangaw in Magway, hot in nearly every
quarter but with a significantly falling trend.

**No persistent hot spots.** No township was a significant hot spot in 90% of the
19 quarters. Again the reason is the window: the first quarter or two predate the
resistance in exactly the places that later became its core.

### Interpreting the cold spot classes

Cold spots are 138 townships, more than the hot spots, and they are of two kinds.
The **persistent cold spots** (`r sum(ehsa_pv$classification == "persistent coldspot")`)
are almost all in the Shan hills: 21 of them in eastern, northern and southern
Shan. That area contains the Wa and Mongla zones, where I argued in the data audit
that zeros partly measure silence. The **consecutive cold spots**
(`r sum(ehsa_pv$classification == "consecutive coldspot")`) are all in Yangon:
townships that were not significantly cold in the first years and have been
continuously cold since, the same cooling the Mann-Kendall map shows.
The single **intensifying cold spot**, Kunhing in southern Shan, records only eight
events.

The large **sporadic cold spot** group (`r sum(ehsa_pv$classification == "sporadic coldspot")`)
is mostly the Ayeyarwady delta and Yangon, the military's most secure territory: places that are sometimes significantly quiet
relative to the national level. It would be a mistake to read "cold spot" as "safe".
A cold spot in Yangon is a place where armed clashes are rare. It is also a place
where repression takes forms ACLED records as arrests and strategic developments,
which I excluded.

## By event type

```{r fig-ehsa-types}
#| fig-cap: "EHSA classes by event type, all classes shown. Explosions and remote violence share the dry-zone pattern of the total; battles carry a stronger border signal; violence against civilians has no intensifying hot spot at all."
#| fig-height: 6.4
et <- with_geo(E$ehsa |> filter(var != "pv")) |>
  mutate(var = var_lab(var), classification = factor(classification, EHSA_LEVELS))
present_t <- levels(droplevels(et$classification))
ggplot(et) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = classification), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.04) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.18) +
  facet_wrap(~var, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(18)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = EHSA_COLS()[present_t], breaks = present_t,
                    labels = ehsa_label(present_t), name = NULL) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(12, "pt"))
```

The three types tell slightly different stories. **Battles** produce the most
consecutive hot spots, front by front, and eight intensifying cold spots, all in
central Yangon and the delta, where armed clashes occurred in 2021 and then stopped
almost entirely.
**Explosions and remote violence** reproduce the dry-zone pattern of the total, with
its own six intensifying hot spots, consistent with the air campaign concentrating
on the resistance heartland. **Violence against civilians** has no intensifying
hot spot, and the most townships with no pattern at all: it is diffuse in time,
following raids and sweeps rather than fixed fronts.

## Reading individual trajectories

```{r fig-traj}
#| fig-cap: "The space-time Gi* series that EHSA classified, for one township from several classes. Solid points are significant at p < 0.05. The dashed lines are the coup and Operation 1027."
#| fig-height: 4.8
pick <- c("Madaya", "Kawkareik", "Monywa", "Hlaingtharya (East)", "Gangaw", "Kunhing")
pick <- intersect(pick, tsp$TS)
tr <- G |> left_join(tsp_attr, by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  filter(TS %in% pick) |>
  left_join(ehsa_pv |> select(TS, classification), by = "TS") |>
  mutate(lab = glue("{TS}: {ehsa_label(classification)}"))
ggplot(tr, aes(period, gi)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$rule) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(COUP_DATE, OP1027_DATE), colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.25, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = classification, alpha = p_sim < ALPHA), size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = EHSA_COLS(), guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.25), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~lab, ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gi*") + theme_ex02(base_size = 10)
```

The trajectories make the labels concrete. Monywa and Madaya are both
significantly cold in the coup quarter and hot in almost every quarter after it;
Monywa's Gi* levels off, Madaya's keeps climbing, and that difference alone puts one
in "oscillating" and the other in "intensifying". Kawkareik is not significant
through 2021 and then hot in every quarter from 2022 onward, an unbroken final run
that makes it "consecutive". Gangaw is hot almost throughout but drifting down.
Hlaingtharya (East), an industrial township on Yangon's western edge, is hot in
2021 and cold by the end. Kunhing in southern Shan is cold in all 19 quarters and
getting colder.

## Sensitivity of the classification {#sec-ehsa-sens}

```{r}
#| include: false
agree_coarse <- function(b, o) mean(coarse(b$classification) == coarse(o$classification[match(b$TS_PCODE, o$TS_PCODE)]))
base_pv <- E$ehsa |> filter(var == "pv")
ac_m <- agree_coarse(base_pv, E$sens$ehsa_m); ac_r <- agree_coarse(base_pv, E$sens$ehsa_raw)
```

EHSA classes are less stable than the local statistics, and this needs saying
plainly. Rebuilding the cube monthly keeps the same class for
`r fmt_pct(E$sens$agree_month)` of townships; using raw counts instead of
log(1 + count) keeps it for `r fmt_pct(E$sens$agree_raw)`. At the coarser level of
hot, cold or neither, agreement rises to `r fmt_pct(ac_m)` and `r fmt_pct(ac_r)`.
Most of the movement is between neighbouring classes: sporadic hot spots in the
quarterly cube become "no pattern" in the monthly one, because monthly noise makes
an occasional significant quarter harder to reach. Intensifying hot spots either
stay intensifying or become oscillating, never cold.

So I read the EHSA results at two levels. The broad geography (which townships are
hot, which cold, which are trending) is robust. The fine distinctions between
sporadic, oscillating and consecutive depend on parameter choices and should be
used to prompt a look at the trajectory, not quoted as fact.

# Value-added analysis: does violence spread? {#sec-diffusion}

## The question

EHSA describes where hot spots appear and persist. It does not say *how* a quiet
township becomes violent. For a peace-building organisation that is the question
that matters for planning: if violence spreads to neighbours, the townships to
prepare are the quiet ones on the edge of active areas; if it jumps or appears
independently, adjacency is no guide.

The conflict literature distinguishes contagious diffusion, where violence spreads
to adjacent places, from relocation, where it moves and leaves its origin quiet
(Schutte and Weidmann 2011). I test the first with a spatial Markov chain (Rey 2001).

## Method

Each township-quarter is classified **Active** if it records at least
`r ACTIVE_MIN` political-violence events (one a month, which separates sustained
activity from an isolated incident) and **Quiet** otherwise. Each township's
neighbourhood in that quarter is classified by the share of its queen neighbours
that are active: none, some (under half), or most (half or more). I then estimate
the probability of being Active in the next quarter, conditional on the township's
own state and its neighbourhood. That gives `r fmt_n(nrow(D$tr))` observed
transitions.

If violence diffuses contagiously, a quiet township's chance of becoming active
should rise with its neighbours' activity.

## Result

```{r fig-markov}
#| fig-cap: "Probability that a township is active in the next quarter, by its own state and its neighbours'. Bars give the full period; points split it at Operation 1027. n is the number of township-quarter transitions behind each bar."
#| fig-height: 4.2
pt <- D$phase_tab |> mutate(ctx = factor(ctx, D$ctx_lab))
tb2 <- D$tab |> mutate(ctx = factor(ctx, D$ctx_lab))
ggplot(tb2, aes(ctx, p_active_next)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 0.62) +
  geom_point(data = pt, aes(shape = phase, colour = phase), size = 2.4,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.38)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = glue("n = {fmt_n(n)}"), y = 0.02), vjust = 0, size = 2.6,
            colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(from, c("Quiet", "Active"), c("Quiet this quarter", "Active this quarter"))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(PAL$cool, PAL$accent_dk), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("None", "Some", "Most")) +
  labs(x = "Neighbours active this quarter", y = "Active next quarter") + theme_ex02()
```

A quiet township with no active neighbour becomes active in the next quarter
`r fmt_pct(on_none)` of the time. With most neighbours active, the figure is
`r fmt_pct(on_most)`, about four times higher. The same gradient appears for
active townships: an active township with no active neighbours stays active about
half the time, but one surrounded by fighting stays active
`r fmt_pct(tb$p_active_next[tb$from == "Active" & tb$ctx == D$ctx_lab[3]])` of the time.
The likelihood-ratio test of homogeneity across neighbourhoods rejects
decisively (G² = `r round(D$lr$G2)`, `r D$lr$df` df).

## Is it contagion, or just a violent region?

The likelihood-ratio test assumes every transition is independent, which is false:
each township contributes 18 transitions, and neighbouring townships share
conditions. Three checks address this.

**Spatial permutation.** I kept every township's full 19-quarter history intact
and shuffled which location each history sits at, 499 times, recomputing the
onset gap each time. This destroys spatial arrangement while preserving every
township's temporal persistence.

```{r fig-perm}
#| fig-cap: "Onset gap (most neighbours active minus none active) under 499 spatial permutations, against the observed gap."
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(tibble(g = D$gap_perm), aes(g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = PAL$null, colour = PAL$border) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = D$gap_obs, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = D$gap_obs, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1.05, size = 3,
           label = glue("observed {round(100 * D$gap_obs)} points"), colour = PAL$accent,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(round(100 * x), " pts")) +
  labs(x = "Onset gap under random placement", y = NULL) + theme_ex02()
```

Not one permutation reaches the observed gap (p `r fmt_p(D$p_perm, 499)`). Under
random placement the gap is centred slightly *below* zero, because shuffling places
busy townships next to quiet ones.

**Controlling for region and time.** A logistic model of onset among quiet
townships with fixed effects for each of the 18 states and regions and for each
quarter, plus the township's own activity in the previous year, still finds
the neighbourhood effect (@tbl-or). A township with most neighbours active has
`r round(or_most$OR, 1)` times the odds of onset of one with none, with a
township-cluster bootstrap interval of `r round(or_most$lo, 1)` to
`r round(or_most$hi, 1)`. The effect cannot be "this is Sagaing" or "this was a
violent quarter", because those are held constant.

```{r tbl-or}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Odds ratios for onset (Quiet to Active) among quiet township-quarters. Fixed effects for state/region and quarter not shown. Intervals are 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 200 bootstrap fits resampling whole townships."
D$or_tab |> mutate(Term = recode(term, "ctxSome neighbours active" = "Some neighbours active (vs none)",
                                 "ctxMost neighbours active" = "Most neighbours active (vs none)",
                                 "hist4TRUE" = "Own activity in previous four quarters"),
                   `Odds ratio` = round(OR, 2), `95% interval` = glue("{round(lo, 2)} to {round(hi, 2)}")) |>
  select(Term, `Odds ratio`, `95% interval`) |> kable()
```

**Threshold.** The gradient holds whatever "active" means:

```{r tbl-thr}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Onset probability by neighbourhood for three definitions of an active township-quarter."
D$thr_sens |> transmute(`Active means at least` = glue("{threshold} event{if_else(threshold > 1, 's', '')} per quarter"),
                        `Township-quarters active` = fmt_pct(share_active),
                        `No neighbour active` = fmt_pct(none), `Some` = fmt_pct(some),
                        `Most` = fmt_pct(most), Ratio = round(ratio, 1)) |> kable()
```

## What changed with Operation 1027

```{r}
#| include: false
ph <- function(phase, ctx) D$phase_tab$p_active_next[D$phase_tab$from == "Quiet" &
                                                     D$phase_tab$phase == phase & D$phase_tab$ctx == ctx]
b_none <- ph("Before Operation 1027", D$ctx_lab[1]); a_none <- ph("From Operation 1027", D$ctx_lab[1])
b_most <- ph("Before Operation 1027", D$ctx_lab[3]); a_most <- ph("From Operation 1027", D$ctx_lab[3])
```

Splitting the transitions at Operation 1027 (the points in @fig-markov) shows a
chain that is not stationary, and the way it changes is informative. Before the
offensive, a quiet township with no active neighbours ignited
`r fmt_pct(b_none)` of the time; from 2023 Q4 onward, `r fmt_pct(a_none)`. Onset
next to active neighbours did not change at all (`r fmt_pct(b_most)` before,
`r fmt_pct(a_most)` after). Isolated outbreaks have become rare. New violence now
appears almost only at the edge of existing violence. That is what a war of
consolidated fronts and contested territory looks like, as opposed to the scattered
uprising of 2021 and 2022.

## Does the neighbourhood help predict?

A statistically significant effect is not the same as a useful one. I fitted the
onset model on transitions up to mid-2024 and scored the four later quarters,
comparing it with a model that knows only each township's own history and state.

```{r tbl-oos}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample discrimination for onset among quiet townships, transitions starting 2024 Q3 to 2025 Q2. AUC is the probability that a township that did become active was ranked above one that did not."
D$oos |> transmute(Model = model, AUC = round(auc, 3),
                   `Test transitions` = fmt_n(n_test), Onsets = onsets) |> kable()
```

The neighbourhood adds a modest `r round(D$oos$auc[2] - D$oos$auc[1], 3)` to the
AUC. Most of what predicts onset is already known to anyone watching a township's
own recent history. The neighbourhood is a useful second signal, not a forecasting
system, and I would not present it as more than that.

## Quiet townships on the edge

```{r fig-watch}
#| fig-cap: "Townships that were quiet in 2025 Q3 (fewer than three events), shaded by the share of their neighbours that were active. Active townships are shown in grey. The darkest quiet townships are the ones the diffusion result says to watch."
#| fig-height: 7.4
#| fig-width: 7
wm <- with_geo(D$watch |> select(TS_PCODE, share, p_onset))
ggplot(wm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = share), colour = PAL$border, linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#EEF6F7", PAL$cool_lt, "#E7B9A9", PAL$accent),
                       na.value = "#C9CBD0", labels = label_percent(),
                       name = "Quiet townships: share of neighbours active, 2025 Q3") +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE, datum = NA) + theme_map() +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(40, "pt"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
w_most <- D$watch |> filter(ctx == D$ctx_lab[3])
w_st <- w_most |> count(ST, sort = TRUE)
```

In the last observed quarter, `r nrow(D$watch)` townships were quiet, and
`r nrow(w_most)` of them had most of their neighbours active. They cluster in
`r paste(glue("{w_st$ST[1:4]} ({w_st$n[1:4]})"), collapse = ", ")`: the margins of
the dry-zone and southern fronts. The map is a list of where the diffusion result
says to look, not a forecast, and it inherits every limitation of ACLED's coverage.

# Integrated findings and discussion

The methods agree on one picture.

**Where.** Myanmar's armed conflict since the coup is centred on the dry zone of
Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay, with a second belt down the eastern border from Bago
East to Tanintharyi. Local Moran's I, Gi*, every event type and every robustness
check put the core in the same place. There are no isolated violent townships;
violence comes in neighbourhoods.

**How it is changing.** The urban resistance of 2021 is gone from the map; Yangon
is cooling almost everywhere. The war has deepened in the dry zone, where the
intensifying hot spots are, and has opened and held new fronts along the
southeast, where the consecutive hot spots run from Kyaukkyi to Myawaddy. Rakhine and
northern Shan are on-and-off theatres that flare with offensives and quiet with
ceasefires. And the means of violence changed: the military's air campaign grew
more than thirtyfold between 2021 and 2024, and explosions and remote violence now
outnumber battles.

**How it spreads.** Violence spreads to neighbours. A quiet township beside active
ones is about four times as likely to become active next quarter as an isolated one,
and that holds after accounting for region, time and the township's own history.
Since Operation 1027 almost all new violence has appeared next to existing
violence.

**What I would not claim.** That the cold spots are peaceful: some are well
reported and secure; others, like the Wa zones, are under-reported. That fine EHSA
labels are stable: the hot/cold geography is, the sub-classes are not. That the
diffusion model forecasts: it ranks quiet townships modestly better than history
alone.

# Peace-building implications

These follow from the analysis. They are not policy recommendations; they are what
the evidence would support if a peace-building organisation asked.

1. **Prioritise the intensifying hot spots for protection and humanitarian access**,
   particularly Madaya, Myingyan, Seikphyu, Yesagyo and Ngazun in the dry zone, and
   Dawei. Their violence is established and still rising. Civilian protection,
   mine-risk education and access negotiation are most needed where conflict is
   neither new nor ending.

2. **Watch the quiet edges, not the centres.** The diffusion result says onset is
   concentrated in quiet townships next to active ones. Early-warning monitoring
   and preparedness (displacement planning, pre-positioned supplies) belong in the
   townships in @fig-watch, which are most numerous in Magway, Sagaing, Kachin and
   Mandalay, before they light up.

3. **Treat the southeastern front as a moving front.** The consecutive hot spots
   from Bago East to the Thai border are places that became hot and stayed hot.
   Cross-border humanitarian routes from Thailand matter most here.

4. **Plan for air-strike exposure where there are no battles.** An air strike lands
   where the military chooses, which need not be where ground fighting is. Civilian
   protection in the dry zone cannot be planned from battle maps alone.

5. **Do not read the eastern Shan cold spot as an absence of risk.** It partly
   reflects how little is reported from Wa and Mongla territory. Field verification
   should come before any programme decision that depends on calm there.

# Limitations

**ACLED measures reporting, not violence.** Every count in this analysis is a count
of events reported in sources ACLED monitors. Reporting is uneven: dense near
media and civil-society networks, thin in ceasefire enclaves, contested hills and
places under communication blackout. Hot spots partly reflect where violence is
visible. The Wa and Mongla zeros are the clearest example; others are likely.

**Counts, not rates.** I have no reliable township population or exposure
denominator for 2021-2025. Large or populous townships may record more events for
reasons other than intensity. Gi* and Local Moran's I compare neighbourhoods, which
softens this, but does not remove it.

**The modifiable areal unit problem.** Townships range from under 1 km² in central
Yangon and Mandalay to over 12,000 km². Clusters at township scale need not exist at village tract or district
scale. I chose townships because programmes operate at that level, not because
the clusters are scale-free.

**Contiguity is a simplification.** Queen contiguity treats every shared border as
an equal channel. Mountain ranges, rivers and front lines make some borders far
more permeable than others. The nearest-neighbour check shows the core results
are not sensitive to the definition, but none of these definitions is the true
one.

**EHSA and the window.** EHSA classes depend on the study window. Starting in
January 2021, one month before the coup, shapes the "oscillating" labels in the
dry zone. And with 19 quarters, the 90% rule for persistent classes requires a
township to be significant in at least 18 of them, which is a high bar.

**Multiple testing.** Maps at p < 0.05 contain false positives. About half of the
significant townships survive a false discovery rate correction; those are the
cores of the clusters.

**The diffusion model is descriptive.** It shows that onset is concentrated next to
existing violence after controlling for region and time. It does not prove that
violence in one township causes violence in its neighbour: an advancing front and
a contagious process look alike at quarterly resolution. The out-of-sample gain is
small, and the in-sample probabilities in @fig-watch are not validated forecasts.

# Reproducibility

The analysis runs as five scripts that cache to `data/derived/`; this page and the
executive summary only read those caches.

```{r tbl-pipeline}
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Pipeline. Run from Take-home_Ex/Take-home_Ex02/."
tribble(
  ~Script, ~Does, ~Output,
  "R/00_config.R", "Every parameter: window, event types, precision rule, CRS, weights, permutations, thresholds", "-",
  "R/01_prepare.R", "Fetches MIMU boundaries if absent, audits and cleans ACLED, joins events to townships, builds quarterly and monthly cubes", "prepared.rds",
  "R/02_lmsa.R", "Queen weights with island fix, global Moran's I, Local Moran's I, Gi*, sensitivity", "lmsa.rds",
  "R/03_ehsa.R", "Gi* per quarter, Mann-Kendall, EHSA with location check, monthly and raw-count sensitivity", "ehsa.rds",
  "R/03b_ehsa_gi.R", "Reruns the all-violence EHSA keeping its space-time Gi* series, and confirms the labels are identical", "ehsa_gi.rds",
  "R/04_diffusion.R", "Spatial Markov chain, permutation test, fixed-effects model, out-of-sample check, watch list", "diffusion.rds"
) |> kable()
```

The ACLED file must be placed at `data/raw/aspatial/` by hand (see the README);
everything else runs end to end with `Rscript`. All random procedures are seeded
(`r SEED`).

```{r session}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "R and package versions"
pk <- c("sf", "sfdep", "spdep", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "Kendall", "patchwork")
cat(R.version.string, "\n")
cat(paste(pk, vapply(pk, \(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)), ""), collapse = "\n"))
```
